The upper part illustrates the methodological framework: the water module is expanded and embedded as intermediate inputs into the CGE model (left panel). Based on this extended model, water consumption control policies are simulated (middle panel) to address the problem of low utilization rates of highly mineralized mine water at the Ningdong Energy Chemical Industry Base (right panel). The lower part presents the simulation results from the Ningdong Energy Chemical Industry Base case study. Three policy scenarios are compared: reducing Yellow River water consumption alone increases mine water consumption and water use efficiency, but harms the economy (left panel); increasing mine water consumption alone unexpectedly leads to an increase rather than a decrease in Yellow River water consumption, accompanied by a significant reduction in water use efficiency (right panel); and a combined quota policy (a 3.6% reduction in Yellow River water coupled with an 11.8% increase in mine water) results in only a 0.6% decline in industrial value\u2011added while improving water use efficiency by 8.45% (middle panel). The graphic visually demonstrates that the combined quota policy achieves the best balance between economic performance and water use efficiency, making it an effective tool for water security management in arid regions. Key variables shown include industrial value\u2011added, water consumption volumes, and water use efficiency indicators under different policy scenarios.<\/jats:p>\n                  <jats:p>With the expansion of coal and other related water-intensive industries in the arid region of Northwest China, the region's already fragile water resources system faces an even greater challenge. Reducing conventional water consumption and increasing unconventional water consumption in water-intensive industries are effective measures for solving water problems. This article takes the Ningdong Energy Chemical Industry Base as a case study. Considering the feasibility and the degree of difficulty of substitution relationships between different water sources, this article expands the water module of the computable general equilibrium (CGE) model. Based on the expanded CGE model, this article assesses water consumption control for water-intensive industries in the base: (I) Reducing the Yellow River water consumption of water-intensive industries increases mine water consumption and industrial water use efficiency, but negatively affects industrial value-added. Specifically, industrial value-added decreases by 4.34% under the scenario of an 8% reduction in the Yellow River water consumption. (II) Increasing mine water consumption in water-intensive industries unexpectedly causes an increase in the Yellow River water consumption and greatly reduces industrial water use efficiency, while industrial value-added is not greatly affected (the change is less than one-tenth of the change in mine water use). (III) The water allocation between the Yellow River water and mine water is simulated. The results show that industrial value-added declines only slightly (about 0.6%), whereas water consumption per 10,000 CNY of industrial value-added decreases by about 8.45%, indicating a substantial improvement in water use
